newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland to create new funds to speed up sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Poland to create new funds to speed up sell-offs.

text.p: The Polish government on Tuesday approved a bill on creating new industry-based investment funds to speed up restructuring and sales of some state-owned firms and help finance the reform of the social security system.
"The bill on industrial funds would enable us to combine mass privatisation and the social security reform," deputy treasury minister Ewa Freyberg told a news conference.

Under the bill, which now goes to parliament for approval, the treasury would set up single-industry funds, several in each industry, and allot to them 80 percent of shares of companies from these sectors.

Freyberg said the government was considering earmarking between 75 and 105 companies for the industrial funds programme, mainly firms with results worse than enterprises destined for direct sales or the government's convertible bond scheme.
"We are considering firms from the energy, steel, chemical and distillery sectors for the programme," she said.
The funds would oversee their firms' restructuring and privatisation by securing financing, finding strategic investors and floating the firms on the bourse.
The treasury will issue certificates of the funds, convertible into 40 percent of the funds' shares, which will be available to all adult Poles for a modest fee.
Poles will be encouraged to contribute the units to new, independently-managed pension funds, envisaged by the coming social security reform.

"A person who will do this will get an equivalent of 0.4 of the certificate as encouragement," Freyberg said. "People about 50 years of age will get three certificates for the price of one," she added.
She earlier said the units could also be exchanged into shares of the funds, which might enter the Warsaw bourse in more than two years.
Freyberg said the government estimated that each certificate would be worth between 130 and 370 zlotys depending on whether 85 percent or 50 percent of eligible adults buy the units.
Under the bill, the 60-percent stakes of the funds, which would not be exchangeable for the units, could be floated or sold to institutional investors.

The proceeds from the sale would also be used to help foot the bill for the social security reform, estimated to cost more than four billion zlotys annually for more than 20 years from the reform's start expected in 1999.
The new scheme has drawn on experience gained from implementing the National Investment Funds scheme, under which 512 firms had been handed over to 15 funds.
